topics.title: Access Control
topics.description: Access control defines who can perform which actions on which cloud resources. It is implemented through identity systems, permission policies, and role assignments. Getting access control right means following the principle of least privilege: every user, service, and system gets exactly the permissions it needs and nothing more.

topics.title: AI/ML Services
topics.description: Cloud providers offer managed AI and machine learning services that remove the need to build and maintain ML infrastructure from scratch. These range from pre-trained model APIs (vision, speech, translation, natural language) to fully managed training and serving platforms (SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML). GPU and TPU instances handle compute-intensive training workloads. Managed vector databases, embedding APIs, and inference endpoints have become standard parts of the cloud AI stack alongside traditional ML pipelines.
resources: What is AI in cloud computing?
AI and Machine Learning with Google Cloud
AWS' AI/ML services Explained in 5 minutes
Managing AI Models in Azure Machine Learning

topics.title: Artifact Registries
topics.description: An artifact registry stores versioned build outputs produced by CI pipelines: container images, compiled binaries, and software packages. Registries sit between the build system and deployment targets, ensuring that what gets deployed is immutable, traceable, and consistent across environments. AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry, and Azure Container Registry are the main managed options. Access control, vulnerability scanning, and image signing are standard features in production registries.
resources: What Is Artifact Registry? | DevOps Academy

topics.title: Auto Scaling
topics.description: Auto scaling automatically adjusts the number of running instances based on demand. A scaling policy monitors a metric (CPU utilization, request rate, queue depth) and triggers the addition or removal of instances to match load. Auto scaling groups in AWS, managed instance groups in GCP, and scale sets in Azure implement this pattern. It is the primary mechanism for achieving elasticity in cloud architectures and directly reduces costs by terminating unused capacity during low-traffic periods.
resources: Most Important Cloud Concepts - Episode 3 - Autoscaling

topics.title: AWS
topics.description: AWS (Amazon Web Services) is the largest cloud provider by market share, launched by Amazon in 2006. It offers over 200 services across compute, storage, networking, databases, machine learning, and more, available in regions across every major continent. AWS is the default choice for many organizations and has the broadest ecosystem of third-party integrations and community resources.

topics.title: Azure
topics.description: Microsoft Azure is the second-largest cloud provider, with particular strength in enterprise environments due to its deep integration with Microsoft products such as Active Directory, Office 365, and Windows Server. Azure is the preferred choice for organizations already running Microsoft workloads and has strong hybrid cloud capabilities through services like Azure Arc.

topics.title: Bare Metal Cloud
topics.description: Bare metal cloud gives you exclusive access to a physical server with no hypervisor layer. You get the full resources of the machine without virtualization overhead, which matters for workloads that require maximum I/O performance, low and predictable latency, or cannot run in a virtualized environment due to licensing or compliance constraints. AWS, GCP, and Azure all offer bare metal options alongside their standard VM instances.
resources: What is a bare metal server?
What is a Bare Metal Cloud?
Bare Metal with a Hypervisor vs. Dedicated Host: What's the difference?

topics.title: Block Storage
topics.description: Block storage provides raw storage volumes that attach to instances and behave like physical disks. The operating system formats them with a filesystem and reads and writes to them at the block level. Block storage offers low latency and high IOPS, making it the right choice for database volumes, operating system disks, and any workload that requires fast random read/write access. AWS EBS, Google Persistent Disk, and Azure Managed Disks are the standard managed block storage options.

topics.title: CDN & Edge Caching
topics.description: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) distributes static and cacheable content (images, scripts, video, API responses) to servers located geographically close to end users, reducing latency and offloading traffic from the origin server. Edge caching stores responses at the CDN layer so repeated requests are served without reaching the origin. CloudFront, Cloud CDN, and Azure CDN are the major managed options. CDNs are also used as a first line of defense against DDoS attacks by absorbing traffic at the edge before it reaches origin infrastructure.

topics.title: CI/CD Pipelines
topics.description: A CI/CD pipeline is an automated workflow that runs whenever code changes are committed. Continuous Integration (CI) builds and tests the change to verify it does not break existing functionality. Continuous Delivery (CD) packages the artifact and ensures it is always in a deployable state. Continuous Deployment goes one step further and pushes to production automatically when all checks pass. Cloud providers offer managed pipeline services (AWS CodePipeline, Google Cloud Build, Azure DevOps) that integrate with source control, artifact registries, and deployment targets.
resources: CI/CD Explained | How DevOps Use Pipelines for Automation

topics.title: CI/CD
topics.description: CI/CD (Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery) is the practice of automating the build, test, and deployment of software so that changes can be released reliably and frequently. In cloud environments, CI/CD pipelines integrate with container registries, IaC tools, and orchestration platforms to take code from a developer's commit to a running production workload with minimal manual steps.
resources: What is CI/CD? Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery
Continuous Integration vs Delivery vs Deployment

topics.title: Cloud Deployment Models
topics.description: Cloud deployment models represent the specific environment where cloud resources, such as servers, storage, and networking, are hosted and made accessible to users. These models define who owns the infrastructure, how it is managed, and the level of control and security available to the organization. The primary categories include public clouds, which are managed by third-party providers over the internet; private clouds, which are dedicated to a single organization; and hybrid clouds, which combine both environments to allow data and applications to be shared between them.
resources: Selecting the right cloud for workloads
Public, Private & Hybrid cloud deployment models

topics.title: Cloud Service Models
topics.description: Cloud service models are standardized frameworks that define the different ways computing resources, applications, and infrastructure are delivered to users over the internet. These models—primarily Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS)—categorize services based on how much control the provider manages versus the user. By selecting a specific model, organizations can choose the appropriate level of abstraction, ranging from full control over virtual hardware to simply consuming a finished software product.
resources: PaaS versus IaaS versus SaaS versus CaaS: How are they different?
IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS cloud service models
Cloud Computing Services Models - IaaS PaaS SaaS Explained

topics.title: Cloud vs On-Premises
topics.description: On-premises infrastructure means owning and operating physical servers in your own data center or server room. Cloud infrastructure means renting virtualized resources from a provider who manages the physical layer. The trade-off is control versus convenience: on-premises gives full hardware control and predictable costs at scale, while cloud offers speed, elasticity, and lower upfront investment.
resources: What is On-Premises Data Centers vs. Cloud Computing?
On Premise vs Cloud : Is Cloud Computing the future?

topics.title: Cluster
topics.description: A cluster is a group of servers (or instances) that work together as a single system. Clusters are used to distribute workloads, provide redundancy, and scale horizontally. Kubernetes clusters, database clusters, and Hadoop clusters are common examples in cloud environments.
resources: How Clusters Work in Distributed Systems: A Deep Dive

topics.title: Configuration Management
topics.description: Configuration management tools manage the state of software and settings on existing servers. Ansible, Chef, and Puppet are the main tools. Where IaC provisions infrastructure, configuration management configures what runs on it: installing packages, writing config files, managing services, and enforcing a desired system state. In cloud environments, configuration management is most relevant for managing fleets of VMs; container-based workloads largely replace it with immutable images built at CI time.
resources: Why You Need to Learn Configuration Management

topics.title: Container Orchestration
topics.description: Container orchestration automates the deployment, scaling, networking, and lifecycle management of containers across a cluster of machines. Running containers in production at scale requires scheduling containers onto nodes with available resources, restarting failed containers, routing traffic to healthy instances, rolling out updates without downtime, and scaling based on load. Orchestration platforms handle all of this through declarative configuration, letting teams focus on application logic rather than operational mechanics.

topics.title: Containers
topics.description: Containers are lightweight, standalone, and executable software packages that include everything needed to run an application, such as code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings. They ensure that software runs reliably and consistently regardless of the computing environment. This approach isolates applications from the underlying infrastructure, allowing them to start quickly, share the host system's kernel, and move seamlessly between different development, testing, and production environments.

topics.title: Control Loops & Controllers
topics.description: The core operating principle of Kubernetes is the control loop. A controller watches the current state of a resource, compares it to the desired state defined in the spec, and takes corrective action if they differ. If a Deployment specifies three replicas and only two are running, the controller creates a third. This reconciliation loop runs continuously, making Kubernetes self-healing by design. Custom controllers and operators extend this pattern to manage application-specific resources using the same model.

topics.title: Core Networking
topics.description: Core networking covers the fundamental building blocks of a cloud network: isolated virtual networks, subnet segmentation, routing, and address management. These are configured before any workload is deployed and form the foundation that all other networking features build on.

topics.title: Cost Monitoring and Budgets
topics.description: Cloud costs are dynamic and can grow unexpectedly as workloads scale or resources are left running. Cost monitoring tools (AWS Cost Explorer, GCP Cost Management, Azure Cost Analysis) provide visibility into spending by service, region, tag, and time period. Budget alerts notify teams when spending approaches or exceeds a defined threshold. Tagging resources consistently is the foundation of cost attribution: without tags, it is difficult to attribute costs to teams, projects, or environments.
resources: Managing your costs with AWS Budgets
Tutorial: Create and manage budgets in Azure

topics.title: Cybersecurity Basics
topics.description: Cybersecurity basics covers the core concepts a cloud practitioner needs before working with security services: what encryption is and how it works, what a firewall does, what a certificate is and why it matters, and the difference between authentication and authorization. Cloud environments expose a large attack surface, and knowing the vocabulary makes the security sections of the roadmap approachable.
resources: What Is Cloud Security? - Google Cloud
Harvard CS50’s Intro to Cybersecurity – Full University Course

topics.title: DaaS
topics.description: DaaS (Desktop as a Service) delivers a virtual desktop environment from the cloud to any device with a browser or thin client. The provider hosts and manages the underlying infrastructure, operating system, and desktop software. It is used by organizations that need to provide a consistent, secure desktop experience to remote or distributed workforces without managing physical machines.
resources: What is desktop as a service (DaaS)?
Introduction to Desktop-as-a-Service | Desktop as a Service (DaaS) | Examples & Advantages

topics.title: Data Archiving
topics.description: Data archiving is the long-term retention of data that is rarely accessed but must be preserved for compliance, legal, or historical purposes. Archive storage classes are designed for this use case, offering very low storage costs in exchange for slow retrieval. Archiving strategies include setting lifecycle rules to move aging data to archive tiers, enabling retention locks to prevent deletion before a defined period, and maintaining audit trails for regulatory compliance.
resources: What Is Data Archiving? Benefits and Considerations
Understanding the Difference Between Backing Up and Archiving

topics.title: Data Centers
topics.description: Data centers are physical facilities that house a centralized collection of servers, networking equipment, and storage systems used to process, store, and distribute massive amounts of data. These buildings provide the necessary infrastructure, such as redundant power supplies, climate control, and high-speed connectivity, to ensure that computing hardware operates reliably around the clock.
resources: What is Data Center Infrastructure? – Data Center Fundamentals

topics.title: Data Lifecycle
topics.description: Data lifecycle management controls how stored data moves, ages, and is eventually retired or preserved. Cloud providers offer tiered storage classes that automatically shift data to cheaper storage as it ages, along with tools to enforce retention periods, prevent premature deletion, and meet regulatory requirements for long-term data preservation.
resources: Cloud data lifecycle: a deep dive

topics.title: Data Protection
topics.description: Data protection covers the controls that keep sensitive data secure at rest, in transit, and throughout its lifecycle. In cloud environments, this includes encryption, secrets management, and compliance with privacy regulations. These controls apply across storage, databases, APIs, and any service that handles customer or business data.
resources: Why backup should be a part of your cyber resilience plan?
Data Security: Protect your critical data (or else)

topics.title: Databases
topics.description: Databases in the cloud are available as managed services, where the provider handles provisioning, patching, backups, replication, and failover. This removes the operational burden of running database software on EC2 instances or bare metal, though it reduces configurability. Most cloud architectures use a mix of database types depending on the access patterns and consistency requirements of each workload.
resources: Cloud databases explained: benefits, challenges, and best practices
What is DBaaS? Should you use it?

topics.title: Deployment Strategies
topics.description: Deployment strategies control how new application versions are released to minimize risk and downtime. A blue/green deployment maintains two identical environments and switches all traffic from old to new instantly, with fast rollback by switching back. A canary deployment routes a small percentage of traffic to the new version first, monitors for errors, and gradually increases the percentage before full rollout. Rolling deployments replace instances one at a time. Each strategy trades deployment speed for risk control.
resources: Deployment strategies: Types, trade-offs, and how to choose
CI/CD deployment: top 6 strategies and how to make them work

topics.title: Developer-Focused
topics.description: Developer-focused cloud providers simplify deployment and operations for smaller teams and individual developers. DigitalOcean, Render, and Fly fall into this category. They offer a streamlined experience with fewer services but lower operational complexity, clear pricing, and good developer tooling. Often the right choice for startups, side projects, and teams without dedicated infrastructure engineers.

topics.title: Distributed Systems
topics.description: A distributed system is a group of independent machines that communicate over a network and work together as one system. Most cloud services are built this way, from load-balanced servers to replicated databases. Distribution brings scale and fault tolerance, but also network delays, partial failures and data consistency trade-offs such as the CAP theorem.
resources: Distributed Systems Explained | System Design Interview Basics

topics.title: DNS in the Cloud
topics.description: Cloud DNS services resolve domain names to cloud resources and go beyond basic A record management. They support latency-based routing (directing users to the nearest region), geolocation routing, weighted routing for gradual traffic shifts, and health-check-based failover that automatically removes unhealthy endpoints. Route 53, Cloud DNS, and Azure DNS integrate directly with load balancers, CDNs, and other cloud services to enable these traffic patterns.
resources: What is DNS? | How DNS works
How a DNS Server (Domain Name System) works.

topics.title: Docker
topics.description: Docker is the most widely used container platform. It provides a CLI and daemon for building container images, running containers, and managing their lifecycle on a single host. A Dockerfile defines the steps to assemble an image: base OS, dependencies, application code, and startup command. Docker also introduced the image registry model, with Docker Hub as the public registry, which became the foundation for how container images are distributed and versioned.
resources: Docker Crash Course for Absolute Beginners

topics.title: Edge Computing
topics.description: Edge computing moves compute closer to where data is generated or consumed, rather than sending everything to a centralized cloud region. This reduces latency for time-sensitive workloads and lowers bandwidth costs by processing data locally before sending summaries or results to the cloud. Edge nodes can be CDN points of presence, on-premises hardware, or small cloud deployments in regional facilities.
resources: What is Edge Computing - Cloudflare Docs
What is Edge Computing? Is It More Than a Buzzword?

topics.title: Edge vs Cloud
topics.description: Cloud computing centralizes compute in large, efficient data centers with global reach but introduces latency for users and devices far from those regions. Edge computing distributes compute to locations near the source of data or the end user, reducing round-trip time at the cost of smaller, less powerful hardware and more complex operations. The two are complementary: edge handles latency-sensitive or bandwidth-heavy processing locally, while cloud handles storage, analytics, and workloads where centralization is an advantage.
resources: What’s the Difference Between Edge Computing and Cloud Computing?
Edge Computing Vs. Cloud Computing - Key Differences to Know | Intellipaat

topics.title: Elasticity
topics.description: Elasticity is the ability of a system to automatically provision and release resources in response to demand. A highly elastic system scales out when traffic increases and scales back in when it drops, paying only for what it uses. Elasticity is one of the defining properties of cloud computing and the basis for auto scaling and serverless architectures.
resources: What is elasticity in cloud computing?
What is Scalability and Elasticity in Cloud Computing?

topics.title: Encryption
topics.description: Encryption protects data by transforming it into an unreadable format that can only be decoded with the correct key. Encryption at rest protects stored data (in databases, object storage, disk volumes) from unauthorized access if physical or logical storage is compromised. Encryption in transit protects data moving over networks using TLS, preventing interception. Cloud providers encrypt managed services by default and offer key management services (AWS KMS, Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault) for managing and rotating encryption keys.
resources: What is Cloud Encryption & Why is it Important?

topics.title: Endpoint
topics.description: An endpoint is a URL or network address where a service can be reached. Cloud services expose endpoints for APIs, storage buckets, databases, and load balancers. Endpoints can be public (accessible from the internet) or private (accessible only within a VPC). Managing endpoints is a routine part of configuring cloud services and access control.

topics.title: Event-Driven Architecture
topics.description: Event-driven architecture is a design pattern where services communicate by producing and consuming events rather than making direct calls to each other. An event (a file upload, a database write, a user action, a scheduled trigger) causes one or more functions or services to execute in response. This decouples producers from consumers, making systems easier to scale independently and more resilient to partial failures. It is the natural architectural pattern for serverless workloads.

topics.title: FaaS
topics.description: FaaS (Function as a Service) lets you deploy individual functions that run in response to events, with no server management. The provider handles all infrastructure, scaling to zero when idle and scaling out automatically under load. AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, and Azure Functions are the main platforms. FaaS is the compute model behind serverless architectures.
resources: What is function as a service (FaaS)?
What is FaaS (Functions as a Service)?

topics.title: File Storage
topics.description: File storage provides a managed shared filesystem accessible by multiple instances simultaneously over standard protocols like NFS or SMB. Unlike block storage, which is attached to a single instance, file storage can be mounted by many instances at once, making it suited for shared application data, content management systems, and HPC workloads that require a common filesystem. AWS EFS, Google Filestore, and Azure Files are the main managed offerings.
resources: File Storage VS Object Storage | System Design

topics.title: FinOps
topics.description: FinOps (Cloud Financial Operations) is a practice and organizational model for managing cloud spending collaboratively across engineering, finance, and business teams. It brings financial accountability to variable cloud costs by establishing processes for cost visibility, allocation, forecasting, and optimization. FinOps teams define tagging standards, review spending regularly, track unit economics (cost per request, cost per customer), and create feedback loops so engineering teams understand the cost impact of their architectural decisions.
resources: What is FinOps ? | FinOps explained in 10 mins
Adopting FinOps: Stories, Guidance, and Best Practices

topics.title: Firewalls & Security Groups
topics.description: Security groups are stateful virtual firewalls attached to individual instances or network interfaces. They define which inbound and outbound traffic is allowed by port, protocol, and source IP or security group. Network ACLs (Access Control Lists) operate at the subnet level and are stateless, requiring explicit rules for both directions. Together they form the primary traffic filtering layer in a VPC, controlling what can reach your instances and what your instances can reach.
resources: What are Cloud Firewalls and Network Security Groups, and How Do They Secure Workloads in the Cloud?
AWS Security Groups Simply Explained: A Step-by-Step Tutorial for Beginners

topics.title: GCP
topics.description: GCP (Google Cloud Platform) is Google's public cloud, known for its strengths in data analytics, machine learning, and Kubernetes, which Google originally developed. BigQuery, Vertex AI, and Google Kubernetes Engine are among its most widely used services. GCP has a smaller market share than AWS and Azure but is particularly strong in data-intensive and AI-driven workloads.

topics.title: GitOps
topics.description: GitOps is an operational model where Git is the single source of truth for both application and infrastructure configuration. All changes are made through pull requests and code review; automated pipelines detect changes and apply them to the cluster without manual intervention. Tools like ArgoCD and Flux watch a Git repository and continuously reconcile the cluster state with what is defined there. GitOps combines the auditability and collaboration of version control with the automation of IaC and CI/CD.
resources: What is GitOps, How GitOps works and Why it's so useful

topics.title: Hybrid Cloud
topics.description: A hybrid cloud connects private and public cloud environments, allowing workloads to move between them. A common pattern is running sensitive or latency-critical workloads on-premises while using public cloud for burst capacity, backups, or less sensitive services. Hybrid architectures require careful network design and consistent identity and security policies across both environments.

topics.title: Hyperscalers
topics.description: Hyperscalers are cloud providers that operate at massive global scale, with data centers in dozens of regions and hundreds of services covering compute, storage, networking, AI, databases, and more. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure are the three hyperscalers. They set the pace for cloud innovation and account for the majority of global cloud market share.
resources: What is a Hyperscaler Cloud? Top Features and Examples

topics.title: Hypervisors
topics.description: A hypervisor is the software layer that makes virtualization possible. It sits between the physical hardware and the virtual machines running on top of it, allocating CPU, memory, and I/O resources to each VM while keeping them isolated from one another. Type 1 hypervisors (KVM, VMware ESXi, Hyper-V) run directly on bare metal and are used by all major cloud providers. Type 2 hypervisors (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) run on top of a host operating system and are used primarily for local development.

topics.title: IaaS
topics.description: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) gives you raw computing resources over the internet: virtual machines, storage, and networking, without the overhead of managing physical hardware. You control the operating system and everything above it; the provider manages the physical layer. EC2, Google Compute Engine, and Azure Virtual Machines are IaaS products. IaaS is the foundation most other cloud service models build on.

topics.title: IAM
topics.description: IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the system that controls who can access cloud resources and what they can do with them. Every action in a cloud environment (launching an instance, reading a bucket, calling an API) is authorized through IAM. Identities can be human users, service accounts, or cloud services. Policies attached to identities define allowed actions on specific resources. IAM is the foundation of cloud security; misconfigured IAM policies are one of the most common causes of cloud security incidents.
resources: Introduction to Identity and Access Management (IAM)
What is identity and access management (IAM)?

topics.title: Infrastructure as Code
topics.description: Infrastructure as Code treats cloud resources the same way software treats application logic: defined in files, stored in version control, reviewed through pull requests, and applied through automated tooling. It replaces manual console clicks with reproducible, diffable configuration and is the foundation of consistent multi-environment deployments.

topics.title: Instance Types
topics.description: Cloud providers offer a range of instance types to match different workload requirements. Each type provides a specific combination of CPU, memory, storage, and network capacity, organized into families optimized for general use, compute-intensive tasks, memory-heavy applications, or GPU workloads. Selecting the right instance type is one of the most direct levers for managing both performance and cost.
resources: What is Cloud Instance: Types, Benefits & Best Practices

topics.title: Instance
topics.description: An instance is a single virtual server running in the cloud. You choose its size (CPU, memory, storage) from a catalog of instance types and pay for it by the second or hour. Instances are the basic unit of compute in IaaS environments.
resources: What is an Instance In Cloud Computing?
What Is an Instance in Cloud Computing? See How It Powers Your Apps
Cloud Computing Explained: The Most Important Concepts To Know

topics.title: Introduction
topics.description: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing resources over the internet, including servers, storage, databases, networking, and software, provided on demand by third-party providers. Instead of owning and maintaining physical hardware, you rent what you need and pay for what you use. This model shifts infrastructure from a capital expense to an operational one, enabling teams to move f
resources: Cloud Computing Full Course | Cloud Computing Tutorial For Beginners

topics.title: Kubernetes
topics.description: Kubernetes is the standard container orchestration platform. You define workloads as declarative specs (Pods, Deployments, StatefulSets, Services) and Kubernetes continuously reconciles the actual state of the cluster with the desired state. It handles scheduling, self-healing, scaling, service discovery, and rolling updates. All major cloud providers offer managed Kubernetes services (EKS, GKE, AKS) that handle the control plane, leaving teams responsible only for their workloads and node configuration.

topics.title: Latency & Throughput
topics.description: Latency is the time it takes for a single request to travel from sender to receiver and back. Throughput is the amount of data or number of requests a system can handle per unit of time. Both are used to measure and design cloud system performance: low-latency systems respond quickly to individual requests, while high-throughput systems handle large volumes of work efficiently.
resources: What’s the Difference Between Throughput and Latency?
What is Latency? (In about a minute)

topics.title: Levels of Automation
topics.description: Cloud automation exists on a spectrum. At the lowest level, engineers run manual commands through a console or CLI. Scripts automate repetitive tasks but require manual execution. Declarative IaC tools describe desired state and apply it automatically. At the highest level, self-healing systems detect and correct drift without human intervention, using control loops and event-driven automation. Moving up this spectrum reduces toil, improves consistency, and makes infrastructure auditable and repeatable.
resources: The Autonomous Cloud Optimization Spectrum: 6 Levels of Autonomy
What is Cloud Automation? (and why you need to learn it)

topics.title: Lights-Out Operations
topics.description: A lights-out data center is designed to operate without on-site staff. Hardware is monitored, managed, and in many cases repaired remotely through out-of-band management interfaces like IPMI or iDRAC. Cloud providers operate lights-out facilities at scale, reducing labor costs and enabling faster incident response through automation rather than physical intervention.
resources: What is a lights out data center?
The road to automation: Exploring lights-out data centers
The Future of Data Centers: Overcoming the Challenges of Lights-Out Operations
The Entire AI Data Center Explained — From Electricity to ChatGPT

topics.title: Linux
topics.description: Linux is the operating system that runs the vast majority of cloud servers, containers, and managed services. Working in the cloud means reading logs, navigating filesystems, managing processes, and configuring services from a Linux shell. A solid grasp of Linux is assumed across the entire cloud stack.

topics.title: Load Balancers
topics.description: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend instances to prevent any single server from becoming a bottleneck. Layer 4 load balancers operate at the TCP/UDP level and route traffic based on IP and port. Layer 7 load balancers understand HTTP and can route based on URL path, hostname, or request headers, and handle SSL termination and sticky sessions. Cloud providers offer managed load balancers (ALB, NLB on AWS; Cloud Load Balancing on GCP; Azure Load Balancer) that scale automatically and integrate with auto scaling groups.
resources: What is cloud load balancing? | LBaaS

topics.title: Managed Kubernetes
topics.description: Some providers specialize in managed Kubernetes as their primary product, targeting teams that want Kubernetes without the complexity of running it on a hyperscaler. Civo and Vultr are examples. They offer faster cluster provisioning, simpler pricing, and a focused feature set compared to EKS, GKE, or AKS.

topics.title: Managed Relational DBs
topics.description: Managed relational databases provide SQL-compatible storage with ACID guarantees, automatic backups, and multi-AZ failover, without requiring manual database administration. AWS RDS, Google Cloud SQL, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL are examples. They support common engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server) and handle routine maintenance tasks, letting teams focus on schema design and query optimization rather than server management.

topics.title: Microservices Communication
topics.description: Services in a microservices architecture communicate either synchronously or asynchronously. Synchronous communication uses HTTP/REST or gRPC: the caller waits for a response before continuing. Asynchronous communication uses message queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) or event streams (Kafka, Pub/Sub): the caller publishes a message and continues without waiting. Asynchronous patterns improve resilience and decouple services from each other's availability, but make tracing and debugging more complex.
resources: All Microservices Communication Styles in 6 minutes

topics.title: Microservices
topics.description: Microservices is an architectural style that structures an application as a collection of small, independently deployable services, each responsible for a specific business capability and owning its own data store. Services communicate over APIs or message queues rather than sharing a database. The approach enables teams to develop, deploy, and scale services independently, but introduces operational complexity in service discovery, distributed tracing, and failure handling that a monolithic application does not have.
resources: What Are Microservices Really All About? (And When Not To Use It)

topics.title: Monolithic vs Microservices
topics.description: A monolithic application packages all functionality into a single deployable unit. Every feature shares the same codebase, runtime, and database, making it straightforward to develop and test locally but increasingly difficult to scale and deploy as it grows. Microservices decompose the monolith into separate services with clear boundaries. The transition involves trade-offs: microservices improve deployment flexibility and fault isolation but require more sophisticated infrastructure, monitoring, and inter-service communication patterns.
resources: Monolithic vs Microservice Architecture: Which To Use and When?

topics.title: Multi-Cloud
topics.description: Multi-cloud means using services from more than one cloud provider simultaneously. Organizations adopt multi-cloud to avoid vendor lock-in, meet data residency requirements in regions where one provider has no presence, or use best-of-breed services from different providers. It increases operational complexity and requires tooling that works across providers, such as Terraform or Kubernetes.
resources: What is Multicloud? How Do You Manage It?

topics.title: Multi-Tenancy
topics.description: Multi-tenancy means multiple customers share the same physical infrastructure, with each customer's data and workloads isolated from the others. Cloud providers are multi-tenant by default. Isolation is enforced through virtualization, network policies, and IAM controls. Understanding multi-tenancy is important for reasoning about security boundaries and compliance requirements.

topics.title: NAS and SAN
topics.description: NAS (Network Attached Storage) provides file-level storage access over a network, typically using NFS or SMB protocols. SAN (Storage Area Network) provides block-level storage access over a dedicated high-speed fabric, appearing to the server as a locally attached disk. Both technologies predate cloud computing and remain relevant in private cloud and hybrid architectures. Cloud-managed file storage (EFS, Filestore) and block storage (EBS, Persistent Disk) are the cloud equivalents of NAS and SAN respectively.
resources: NAS vs SAN - What are the differences?
What is a Storage Area Network

topics.title: NAT & IP Management
topics.description: Resources in private subnets often need to make outbound requests to the internet (to download updates, call external APIs) without being reachable from outside. A NAT gateway handles this by translating private IP addresses to a public one for outbound traffic. IP management in cloud environments also covers elastic IP allocation (static public IPs), IPv4 vs IPv6 planning, and CIDR block sizing to avoid address space exhaustion as a VPC grows.
resources: Static vs Dynamic NAT: What’s the Difference?
what is an IP Address? // You SUCK at Subnetting // EP 1

topics.title: Network Topology
topics.description: A data center's internal network connects thousands of servers and must handle massive volumes of east-west traffic (between servers) in addition to north-south traffic (between servers and the internet). Modern data center networks are designed to be non-blocking, highly redundant, and software-configurable to support the dynamic workloads cloud environments demand.
resources: A Guide to Simple Two-Tier, Three-Tier, and Spine-Leaf Designs

topics.title: Networking Basics
topics.description: Networking basics covers the fundamental concepts that underpin how computers communicate: IP addresses, subnets, ports, protocols (TCP, UDP, HTTP, HTTPS), and DNS. Cloud networking builds directly on these concepts, and without them, topics like VPCs, security groups, and load balancers are difficult to reason about. Understanding what happens when a request travels from a client to a server is the minimum baseline.

topics.title: NoSQL Databases
topics.description: NoSQL databases store data in formats other than relational tables: key-value pairs, documents, wide columns, or graphs. They are designed for horizontal scalability and flexible schemas, making them well suited to workloads with high write volumes, variable data structures, or access patterns that don't fit SQL queries well. DynamoDB, Firestore, Cassandra, and MongoDB Atlas are widely used managed NoSQL options.
resources: SQL vs. NoSQL Databases: What’s the Difference?
SQL vs. NoSQL: What's the difference?

topics.title: Object Storage
topics.description: Object storage stores data as discrete objects, each consisting of the data itself, metadata, and a unique identifier, in a flat namespace without folder hierarchy. Access is through HTTP APIs rather than a filesystem interface. It is designed for massive scale, high durability (typically 11 nines), and low cost per GB. Object storage is the default choice for backups, media files, logs, static website assets, and data lake raw storage. AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage are the primary implementations.

topics.title: PaaS
topics.description: PaaS (Platform as a Service) provides a managed environment for deploying and running applications, abstracting away the underlying infrastructure. You bring your code; the platform handles the runtime, scaling, patching, and availability. Google App Engine, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, and Heroku are PaaS examples. PaaS trades infrastructure control for reduced operational burden.

topics.title: Power & Cooling
topics.description: Data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity and generate significant heat. Power is delivered through redundant feeds, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), and diesel generators to ensure no single failure causes an outage. Cooling systems, including precision air conditioning, liquid cooling, and hot/cold aisle containment, keep hardware within safe operating temperatures and account for a large portion of a data center's energy consumption.
resources: How Data Centers Work: Power, Cooling, and Infrastructure Explained
Energy consumption in data centers: air versus liquid cooling

topics.title: Pricing Models
topics.description: Cloud providers offer several pricing models that trade cost for flexibility and commitment. On-demand pricing charges by the second or hour with no commitment. Reserved and committed-use pricing offers significant discounts in exchange for a term commitment. Spot and preemptible pricing uses spare capacity at steep discounts but with the risk of interruption. Understanding these models is necessary for making informed infrastructure decisions.
resources: Cloud Pricing Models: How to Choose the Right One in 2026

topics.title: Privacy & Compliance
topics.description: Cloud compliance means meeting regulatory and legal requirements for how data is stored, processed, and accessed. Common frameworks include GDPR (EU data privacy), HIPAA (US healthcare data), SOC 2 (service organization controls), and PCI DSS (payment card data). Cloud providers offer compliance-ready services and share audit reports, but customers remain responsible for configuring those services correctly.

topics.title: Private Cloud
topics.description: A private cloud is infrastructure dedicated to a single organization, either hosted on-premises or in a colocation facility. It offers more control over hardware, network configuration, and data residency than public cloud, which matters for certain regulatory or security requirements. Private clouds require significant capital investment and operational expertise to run.
resources: What is a Private Cloud? Private vs. Public Cloud

topics.title: Provider Landscape
topics.description: The provider landscape refers to the ecosystem of companies that supply infrastructure, platforms, and software services over the internet. These organizations, often called Cloud Service Providers (CSPs), manage large-scale data centers and physical hardware, allowing businesses to rent computing power and storage instead of maintaining their own local servers.
resources: Cloud Providers Compared: A Comprehensive Guide to AWS, Azure, and GCP

topics.title: Provider Lock-In
topics.description: Provider lock-in occurs when an application becomes so dependent on a specific cloud provider's proprietary services that migrating to another provider is costly or technically difficult. Deep use of provider-specific services (managed databases, serverless platforms, AI APIs) accelerates lock-in. Strategies to reduce it include using open standards, Kubernetes, and provider-agnostic tools like Terraform, though some degree of lock-in is often an acceptable trade-off for the productivity gains of managed services.
resources: What is vendor lock-in? | Vendor lock-in and cloud computing
What Is Cloud Vendor Lock-In (And How To Break Free)?

topics.title: Provisioning
topics.description: Provisioning is the process of setting up and configuring cloud resources so they are ready to use. This includes creating instances, allocating storage, configuring networks, and applying security policies. Provisioning can be done manually through a console, programmatically via an API, or declaratively through Infrastructure as Code tools.
resources: What is Cloud Provisioning? Process, Types & Best Practices

topics.title: Public Cloud
topics.description: A public cloud is infrastructure owned and operated by a third-party provider and shared across multiple customers. AWS, GCP, and Azure are public clouds. Resources are provisioned on demand over the internet, and the provider is responsible for all physical hardware and data center operations. Public cloud is the default choice for most modern applications due to its scale, global reach, and breadth of managed services.

topics.title: Python
topics.description: Python is a general-purpose programming language widely used for scripting, automation, and interacting with cloud APIs. In a cloud context, it is the go-to language for writing infrastructure automation scripts, Lambda functions, CLI tools, and data pipelines. Most cloud provider SDKs (boto3 for AWS, google-cloud for GCP, azure-sdk for Azure) have first-class Python support.
resources: Day-0 | Python for DevOps Course Syllabus | Learn Python from Basics | #abhishekveeramalla #python

topics.title: Racks, Pods, & Aisles
topics.description: Servers are housed in vertical metal frames called racks. Racks are grouped into pods, a logical unit of co-located racks managed together for power, cooling, and network purposes. Pods are arranged in rows separated by aisles, which are alternated between hot aisles (where servers exhaust heat) and cold aisles (where cooled air is supplied) to maximize cooling efficiency.
resources: What Is a Pod? What Is a Cluster?

topics.title: RBAC
topics.description: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) assigns permissions to roles rather than to individual users. Users or service accounts are then assigned roles, inheriting the permissions those roles define. This simplifies permission management at scale: instead of editing hundreds of individual user policies, you manage a smaller set of roles. Cloud providers implement RBAC through IAM role policies (AWS), IAM roles and bindings (GCP), and Azure Role Assignments. Kubernetes also uses RBAC to control access to cluster resources.
resources: Role-based Access Control (RBAC) vs. Attribute-based Access Control (ABAC)

topics.title: Region, Availability Zone
topics.description: A region is a geographic area where a cloud provider operates one or more data centers, such as us-east-1 or europe-west1. Within a region, availability zones are physically separate data centers connected by low-latency links. Distributing workloads across availability zones protects against single data center failures without the latency of cross-region replication.

topics.title: Regional Cloud
topics.description: Regional cloud providers operate in specific geographies and are often chosen for data residency, latency, or cost reasons. Examples include Hetzner and OVH in Europe, and UpCloud in the Nordics. They typically offer core IaaS services at competitive prices but with a smaller service catalog and fewer managed offerings than hyperscalers.
resources: Sovereign, Open and Built for Safe AI Agents

topics.title: Resource Optimization
topics.description: Resource optimization reduces cloud spend by eliminating waste and right-sizing infrastructure. Common patterns include terminating unused instances and idle resources, downsizing over-provisioned instances based on actual utilization data, using auto scaling to avoid paying for unused capacity, and replacing always-on instances with serverless or spot workloads where appropriate. Cloud providers offer optimization recommendations (AWS Compute Optimizer, GCP Recommender) that identify specific resources to resize or delete.
resources: Cloud Resource Optimization: Best Practices & Example

topics.title: Retention & Compliance
topics.description: Data retention policies define how long data must be stored and when it can or must be deleted. Compliance requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, PCI DSS) impose specific rules on data storage duration, access controls, encryption, and audit logging. Cloud providers offer services to help meet these requirements: S3 Object Lock, GCS Retention Policies, and Azure Immutable Blob Storage enforce write-once-read-many (WORM) retention, while audit logging services provide the paper trail regulators require.
resources: Data Retention & Legal Compliance for Enterprise Organizations
Cloud-based Data Retention - What’s the point?

topics.title: SaaS
topics.description: SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers fully managed applications over the internet. The provider handles everything: infrastructure, runtime, application code, and updates. Users access the software through a browser or API without managing anything underneath. Gmail, Salesforce, and Slack are SaaS products. From a cloud computing perspective, SaaS is the highest level of abstraction in the service model stack.

topics.title: Scalability
topics.description: Scalability is the capacity of a system to handle growing demand. Vertical scaling adds more power to a single machine (bigger instance). Horizontal scaling adds more machines. Cloud environments favor horizontal scaling because it avoids single points of failure and can be automated. Scalability is a design property, while elasticity is the mechanism that achieves it dynamically.
resources: Scalable Architecture: A Definition and How-To Guide
Scaling Distributed Systems - Software Architecture Introduction

topics.title: Scaling
topics.description: Scaling is the process of adjusting compute capacity to match demand. Cloud environments support both automatic scaling in response to real-time load and pricing-based strategies that trade reliability guarantees for lower cost. Getting scaling right reduces both over-provisioning (wasted spend) and under-provisioning (degraded performance or outages).
resources: Horizontal Vs. Vertical Scaling: Which Should You Choose?
Vertical Vs Horizontal Scaling: Key Differences You Should Know
System Design Basics: Horizontal vs. Vertical Scaling

topics.title: SDN
topics.description: SDN (Software-Defined Networking) separates the network control plane, which decides where traffic goes, from the data plane, which actually forwards packets. In cloud environments, SDN lets providers manage network topology programmatically, enabling VPCs, dynamic routing, network policies, and virtual appliances without touching physical hardware. OpenFlow is an early SDN protocol; most cloud providers implement proprietary SDN stacks tailored to their infrastructure.

topics.title: Secrets Management
topics.description: Secrets management is the practice of storing, accessing, and rotating sensitive values (API keys, database passwords, certificates, tokens) securely. Hardcoding secrets in application code or environment variables is a common source of security breaches. Dedicated secrets managers (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager) store secrets encrypted, control access through IAM policies, provide audit logs of every access, and support automatic rotation to reduce the blast radius of a compromised credential.
resources: How to Manage Secrets in Web Applications?
Secrets Management: Secure Credentials & Avoid Data Leaks

topics.title: Serverless Computing
topics.description: Serverless computing is a model where the cloud provider manages all infrastructure automatically. You deploy code (functions) that run in response to events, with no servers to provision, patch, or scale. The provider handles execution environment management, scales to zero when idle, and charges only for the compute time consumed during function execution. It shifts the operational model from managing capacity to writing event-driven logic.

topics.title: Serverless Platforms
topics.description: The main serverless platforms are AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Run Functions, and Azure Functions. Each executes code in short-lived, stateless containers triggered by events from the provider's ecosystem: API Gateway requests, S3 uploads, Pub/Sub messages, database streams, and more. They differ in supported runtimes, maximum execution duration, cold start latency, concurrency limits, and how tightly they integrate with other services on the same platform.

topics.title: Service Mesh
topics.description: A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication in a microservices architecture. It manages traffic routing, load balancing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, and mutual TLS encryption between services, without any of that logic living in application code. A sidecar proxy (Envoy is the most common) runs alongside each service and intercepts all traffic. Istio and Linkerd are the main implementations. Service meshes add significant operational complexity and are most justified in large deployments with many services.
resources: What is a Service Mesh (AWS blog)?
What is a Service Mesh (RedHat blog)?

topics.title: Shared Responsibility Model
topics.description: The shared responsibility model defines which security tasks the cloud provider handles and which the customer must handle. The provider is responsible for the security of the cloud: physical infrastructure, hardware, hypervisors, and managed service internals. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: operating systems, application code, data, network configuration, and identity management. The boundary shifts depending on the service model: with IaaS the customer manages more; with SaaS almost everything is the provider's responsibility.
resources: What is the shared responsibility model for cloud security?
The Shared Responsibility Model For Cloud Simplified

topics.title: Shell / Bash
topics.description: Bash is the default shell on most Linux systems and the primary language for writing automation scripts in cloud environments. It is used to chain commands, manage files, interact with CLIs, and automate repetitive tasks. Cloud practitioners use Bash daily when working with tools like the AWS CLI, kubectl, or Terraform.
resources: Shell Scripting Crash Course - Beginner Level

topics.title: SLA
topics.description: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is a contract between a cloud provider and a customer that defines the expected level of service, typically expressed as an uptime percentage. AWS S3, for example, offers a 99.99% availability SLA. SLAs also specify what compensation the provider offers if the target is not met. Understanding SLAs is important when designing for reliability and choosing between services.

topics.title: Spot & Reserved Instances
topics.description: Spot instances (AWS) and their equivalents on other providers (preemptible VMs on GCP, spot VMs on Azure) use spare provider capacity at discounts of up to 90% compared to on-demand pricing, but can be reclaimed with short notice when the provider needs the capacity back. Reserved instances commit to a one or three year term in exchange for a significant discount on on-demand rates. Both pricing models require architectural trade-offs: spot instances demand fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads, while reserved instances require accurate capacity planning.
resources: What’s the Difference Between On-Demand Instances and Reserved Instances?
Reserved Instances vs. Spot Instances: Maximize Your Savings Today
Spot Instances vs. Reserved Instances: Key Differences

topics.title: Stateless Functions
topics.description: Stateless functions are small, single-purpose code segments that process data and return a result without saving any information or "state" from previous executions. Each time the function runs, it treats the request as a completely new event, independent of any prior interactions. Because these functions do not rely on stored data on the local server, they can be easily scaled across multiple instances, allowing cloud platforms to instantly spin up or shut down resources based on real-time demand.

topics.title: Storage Classes & Tiering
topics.description: Cloud object storage services offer multiple storage classes with different cost and retrieval trade-offs. Hot tiers store frequently accessed data at higher cost per GB but with immediate retrieval. Cool and cold tiers are cheaper for data accessed infrequently. Archive tiers (Glacier on AWS, Coldline and Archive on GCP) offer the lowest storage cost but charge retrieval fees and have delays of minutes to hours. Lifecycle policies automatically move objects between tiers based on age or access patterns, optimizing cost without manual intervention.
resources: What is Cloud Tiering and How Does it Work?
Choosing the Right Cloud Storage Tier

topics.title: Cloud Storage
topics.description: Cloud storage provides durable, scalable, and managed storage for different types of data and access patterns. Providers offer multiple storage types suited to different use cases: object storage for unstructured data at scale, block storage for low-latency database volumes, and file storage for shared filesystems. Managing the lifecycle and compliance of stored data is as important as choosing the right storage type
resources: What’s the Difference Between Block, Object, and File Storage?
Types of Cloud Storage Explained in 5 minutes - Block, File, Object

topics.title: Subnets & Routing
topics.description: A VPC is divided into subnets, each assigned a CIDR block and typically tied to a specific availability zone. Public subnets have a route to an internet gateway, making resources in them reachable from the internet. Private subnets have no direct internet route and are used for databases, internal services, and anything that should not be publicly accessible. Routing tables define how traffic moves between subnets, to the internet, or to connected on-premises networks.
resources: What is a subnet? | How subnetting works
What is CIDR (Classless Inter Domain Routing)?

topics.title: Terraform
topics.description: Terraform is a provider-agnostic IaC tool that uses a declarative configuration language (HCL) to define infrastructure across AWS, GCP, Azure, and hundreds of other providers. You describe the desired state of your resources, and Terraform calculates a plan showing what it will create, change, or destroy, then applies it. State is stored in a file or remote backend, enabling collaboration and drift detection. Terraform is the dominant tool for multi-cloud and cloud-agnostic infrastructure management.
resources: Terraform explained in 15 mins | Terraform Tutorial for Beginners

topics.title: Trade-offs of Serverless
topics.description: Serverless reduces operational overhead but introduces its own constraints. Cold starts add latency on the first invocation after a period of inactivity, which matters for latency-sensitive applications. Execution time limits (15 minutes on Lambda) rule out long-running processes. Local testing and debugging are harder than with traditional servers. Deep integration with provider-specific event sources and APIs creates significant vendor lock-in. Serverless works best for event-driven, short-lived, and variable-traffic workloads.
resources: Serverless doesn’t mean free: Tradeoffs every engineering team should know
Why serverless? Advantages and disadvantages of serverless computing explained

topics.title: Traffic Management
topics.description: Traffic management controls how requests are routed, distributed, and filtered as they move through a cloud network. It covers DNS resolution, load distribution across instances, network-level security enforcement, and content delivery. These components sit between users and workloads, shaping both performance and availability.
resources: Manage traffic and load for your workloads in Google Cloud
Traffic management with AWS Global Accelerator

topics.title: Upstream Connectivity
topics.description: Upstream connectivity is how a data center connects to the public internet. Providers maintain multiple redundant fiber connections to upstream ISPs and peer directly with other networks at internet exchange points (IXPs) to reduce latency and transit costs. Redundant upstream links ensure that a single cable cut or ISP outage does not take a data center offline.
resources: What is BGP? | BGP routing explained
What is an Internet exchange point? | How do IXPs work?
MicroNugget: What is BGP and BGP Configuration Explained

topics.title: Version Control
topics.description: Version control tracks changes to code and configuration over time, enabling collaboration and rollback. Git is the standard tool. In cloud workflows, version control is the foundation of CI/CD pipelines, Infrastructure as Code practices, and GitOps, where the Git repository is the single source of truth for both application and infrastructure state.

topics.title: Virtual Machine Instances
topics.description: Cloud providers offer a catalog of virtual machine instance types, each with a fixed combination of CPU, memory, and network bandwidth. Instance families are optimized for different workloads: general-purpose instances balance compute and memory, compute-optimized instances have a higher CPU-to-memory ratio for CPU-intensive tasks, memory-optimized instances suit in-memory databases and analytics, and GPU instances are used for machine learning and graphics workloads. Choosing the right instance type directly affects both performance and cost.

topics.title: Virtual Machines
topics.description: A virtual machine is a software-based emulation of a physical computer that runs an operating system and applications just like a dedicated hardware device. By using a hypervisor to partition the resources of a single physical server—such as CPU, memory, and storage—it allows multiple independent virtual machines to operate simultaneously on the same hardware. Each machine functions as a self-contained system, enabling users to run different operating systems or software environments in isolation while sharing the underlying physical infrastructure.
resources: What is a Virtual Machine and how does it work?
Types of Virtual Machines: VM Options for Cloud Computing

topics.title: Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
topics.description: A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is a logically isolated network you define within a cloud provider's infrastructure. Your cloud resources run inside it, invisible to other customers on the same physical hardware. You control the IP address range, subnets, routing tables, and gateways. Every cloud deployment starts with a VPC; it is the network boundary that everything else sits inside.
resources: What Is a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)?
What is a Virtual Network? How it Works and Its Types?
Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) Routing Deep Dive

topics.title: VLANs & VXLAN
topics.description: VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) segment a physical network into isolated logical networks at Layer 2. In large-scale cloud environments, VLANs alone cannot provide enough isolation across distributed data centers. VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) extends Layer 2 networks over a Layer 3 IP fabric by encapsulating Ethernet frames inside UDP packets. It is the underlying technology that enables VPCs and tenant network isolation to scale across thousands of physical hosts.

topics.title: VM Migration, Live Migration
topics.description: VM migration moves a virtual machine from one physical host to another. Standard migration requires the VM to be powered off, causing downtime. Live migration transfers the VM's memory state while it continues running, making the move invisible to users and applications. Cloud providers use live migration for hardware maintenance, load balancing across physical hosts, and fault tolerance when hardware shows signs of failure.
resources: Best Practices for Successful Virtual Machine Migration
Cloud Migration - Options for virtual machines, databases, web apps and containers explained

topics.title: VMs vs Containers
topics.description: Virtual machines virtualize hardware, giving each VM its own OS kernel, which provides strong isolation but comes with significant overhead in memory and startup time. Containers share the host OS kernel and isolate processes using Linux namespaces and cgroups, making them faster to start and more resource-efficient. VMs are preferred when strong isolation or a different OS is required; containers are preferred for running many small, stateless workloads efficiently on shared infrastructure.
resources: Containers vs. VMs: Why not both?
Containers vs VMs: What's the difference?

topics.title: VPN & Direct Connect
topics.description: VPN (Virtual Private Network) tunnels encrypted traffic between an on-premises network and a cloud VPC over the public internet. It is quick to set up and low cost but shares bandwidth with internet traffic. Direct Connect (AWS), Cloud Interconnect (GCP), and ExpressRoute (Azure) provide dedicated private circuits between on-premises infrastructure and the cloud, offering lower and more consistent latency, higher throughput, and no exposure to public internet congestion. Direct connections are used for production hybrid architectures where VPN performance is insufficient.
resources: What is a VPN (virtual private network)?
What Is a Cloud VPN? | Cloud-Based Remote Access VPNs Explained

topics.title: Workload
topics.description: A workload is any application, service, or process running on cloud infrastructure. The term is used to describe what you are running without specifying how: a web application, a batch job, a machine learning training run, and a real-time data pipeline are all workloads. Cloud architecture decisions are often framed around workload characteristics such as latency sensitivity, statefulness, and compute intensity.
resources: Cloud Workloads: Types, Common Tasks, and Security Best Practices

topics.title: Zero Trust
topics.description: Zero Trust is a security model based on the principle of never trust, always verify. No user or system is trusted by default, even if they are inside the corporate network. Every request is authenticated, authorized, and validated against policy before access is granted. In cloud environments, Zero Trust is implemented through strong identity verification, least-privilege IAM policies, network micro-segmentation, and continuous monitoring rather than relying on network perimeter as a trust boundary.
resources: Zero Trust security | What is a Zero Trust network?
